Appendix A Method and Implementation Details

DepGPO redistributes the group-relative advantage of a trajectory using execution dependencies that connect agent commands to verifier-inspected resources. The method traces relevant read and write operations, converts their dependencies into command-level credit, and aggregates these credits into step factors that reweight the advantage over policy-generated tokens. This appendix details the complete procedure, from dependency construction and verifier-based attribution to credit computation, normalization, policy optimization, fallback handling, and end-to-end training.

A.1 Notation and Recorded Events

For task xx, let τi\tau_{i} be the ii-th sampled trajectory and TiT_{i} its number of interaction steps. Step tt consists of an agent response and the resulting environment observation. The set 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} contains the commands associated with that response, and 𝒞i=⋃t𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i}=\bigcup_{t}\mathcal{C}_{i,t} contains all agent commands in the trajectory. The verifier command is denoted by viv_{i} and is not a policy-generated action. Its execution provides the terminal reward RiR_{i} and the resource-access records used to construct the verifier’s read set EiE_{i}. We omit the trajectory index when discussing one trajectory.

Read and write records. We record file accesses, port and process events, and standard output. For file writes, differences between the file contents before and after execution identify the written line ranges when available. In contrast, a file-read record identifies the accessed path without identifying which lines the program uses. Accordingly, writes are tracked at line level, while reads are recorded at file level.

A command with at least one recorded write is a write command, including a command that also reads. This rule also applies to recorded deletions and non-file writes. All remaining commands are read commands. Each traced command receives either write credit or read credit according to its command type. The reads of a write command are still used to construct dependency edges and identify indirect contributions of earlier writes.

Record granularity. When line ranges are available, each tracked written line is identified by its file path and line position. When line ranges are unavailable, the implementation uses the whole-file marker WHOLE_FILE=−1=-1. In that case, the contribution fraction counts file-level fragments. We distinguish this fallback from line-level tracking when reporting examples and statistics.

Path normalization and resource identity. Resource paths are normalized before filtering or matching. Relative paths are resolved against the tracked working directory, while accesses relative to untracked directory descriptors are discarded rather than inferred. Agent and verifier records undergo the same normalization and filtering procedure before dependency construction and extraction of EE. Resources outside the configured work roots and known runtime artifacts are filtered as system noise. Symbolic links are not resolved, so resource identity remains path-based and different aliases of the same underlying file are treated as distinct resources. We regard this as a limitation of the current tracing implementation.

Line ranges and file updates. When available, written line ranges are obtained from the new-side hunks of a per-command file diff and recorded in the file coordinates at the time of execution. Ownership is maintained over (file,line position)(\text{file},\text{line position}) pairs and is not rebased after later insertions or deletions. Consequently, subsequent line shifts may introduce limited positional mismatch in ownership tracking. Renames are represented as deletion of the source path and a write to the destination path, without transferring ownership between the two paths.

Whole-file fallback. When a file-level write is recorded but no usable line range can be recovered, the implementation represents that file with the marker WHOLE_FILE=−1=-1, which contributes one tracked item to 𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{c}. This fallback covers cases such as binary or oversized files, empty-file creation, deletion-only updates, and write sets exceeding the tracing cap. Accordingly, Contrib⁡(c)\operatorname{Contrib}(c) is coarser for such writes than for line-resolved edits, because an unresolved whole-file record contributes a single item to 𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{c}.

Multiple writes within one command. For a command that writes multiple files or disjoint regions, all tracked (file,position)(\text{file},\text{position}) records are pooled into a single set 𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{c}. Thus, |𝒲c||\mathcal{W}_{c}| is computed across all tracked writes of the command, and unrelated written content can reduce its contribution fraction. Any command with at least one recorded write is treated as a write command, even if it also performs reads; these reads remain available for dependency construction and for identifying indirect contributions of earlier writers. Non-file writes such as ports carry no line range and are handled by the binary rules described in Section A.4.

A.2 Construction of the Command Dependency Graph

The graph G=(V,ℰG)G=(V,\mathcal{E}_{G}) contains the agent commands and the verifier command, with V=𝒞∪{v}V=\mathcal{C}\cup\{v\}. A directed edge c→uc\rightarrow u records that a later command uu uses information associated with an earlier command cc. Edges may connect commands from different interaction steps, but never commands from different trajectories.

File dependencies. Commands are processed in execution order. Immediately before command uu is processed, let ou−​(p,ℓ)o_{u^{-}}(p,\ell) denote the latest recorded writer associated with tracked line position ℓ\ell in file pp. File content that has not been written by any agent command has no agent writer and therefore creates no command dependency. When uu reads a file pp, we connect every earlier command that still owns at least one tracked position in pp to uu. Formally,

(c,u)∈ℰfile⟺∃(p,ℓ)such thatp∈ReadFiles(u),ou−(p,ℓ)=c.\displaystyle(c,u)\in\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{file}}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists(p,\ell)\ \text{such that}\ p\in\operatorname{ReadFiles}(u),\quad o_{u^{-}}(p,\ell)=c. (10)

These read dependencies are established before applying the writes of uu. The writes then update ownership of the affected positions, while unaffected positions retain their previous writers. Consequently, multiple earlier commands may remain represented in the same file. An overwrite alone creates no dependency edge between writers; a read of the earlier content is required. Thus, the graph captures recorded read-after-write dependencies rather than write-after-write or write-after-read relations induced solely by execution order.

This processing order applies to the recorded command as a whole. It does not reconstruct the order of individual instructions within a shell command or its subprocesses.

Standard-output dependencies. Standard-output edges capture the reuse of printed information in later command text. The matcher extracts typed values, such as paths and ports, and connects a later command to the first earlier command that printed a matching value of the same type. Values already present in the task description are excluded. This exclusion prevents prompt-provided information from automatically becoming evidence of dependence on an earlier command. When both edge rules connect the same pair of commands, their resource evidence is retained under one mixed edge.

Every edge follows command execution order, making GG acyclic. A read command has no recorded write, and therefore has no outgoing file edge under this construction. Its support for later writes begins with a standard-output edge; subsequent edges on the path may be file edges, standard-output edges, or mixed edges.

A.3 Verifier Read Set and Indirect Write Contributions

The verifier read set defines the resource endpoints used for attribution. After the path normalization and filtering described above, let ℱv\mathcal{F}_{v} denote the files whose contents are read by the verifier, ℬv\mathcal{B}_{v} the files inspected through existence or metadata probes, and 𝒮v\mathcal{S}_{v} the files written by the verifier itself. The file component of the endpoint set is

Efiles=(ℱv∖𝒮v)∪(ℬv∖𝒮v).\displaystyle E_{\mathrm{files}}=(\mathcal{F}_{v}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{v})\cup(\mathcal{B}_{v}\setminus\mathcal{S}_{v}). (11)

Records marked as shadowed by the recorder are removed from the read and probe sets before they are merged. Port and process checks form the remaining components of EE and are not subject to this file-specific filtering. Thus, a resource may belong to EE even when the verifier only probes its existence or metadata rather than reading its contents.

Direct contribution. Let 𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{c} denote the tracked file records written by command cc, represented by file and line position when line-level information is available. Let oend​(p,ℓ)o_{\mathrm{end}}(p,\ell) denote the writer associated with tracked position ℓ\ell in file pp at the end of agent execution. The directly contributing records are

Dc={(p,ℓ)∈𝒲c:p∈Efiles,oend(p,ℓ)=c}.\displaystyle D_{c}=\{(p,\ell)\in\mathcal{W}_{c}:p\in E_{\mathrm{files}},\ o_{\mathrm{end}}(p,\ell)=c\}. (12)

A tracked record therefore receives direct credit when it remains attributed to cc in a file inspected by the verifier. For line-resolved records, this corresponds to written lines that remain in the inspected file at the end of agent execution. The same file-level inspection convention in Eq. 11 applies to verifier probes.

Indirect contribution. A written record that does not remain in an inspected file may still contribute through a later write command. For (p,ℓ)∈𝒲c(p,\ell)\in\mathcal{W}_{c}, let 𝒰c​(p,ℓ)\mathcal{U}_{c}(p,\ell) contain later commands uu satisfying all of the following conditions:

  1. 1.

    uu is a write command and reads file pp;

  2. 2.

    immediately before this read is processed, (p,ℓ)(p,\ell) is still attributed to cc;

  3. 3.

    uu writes to at least one file other than pp; and

  4. 4.

    the writes of uu do not replace the input position (p,ℓ)(p,\ell) being counted.

These conditions provide a conservative rule for indirect attribution. The third condition requires information to propagate beyond the input file, while the fourth excludes earlier content that is replaced by the consuming command itself. Failure to qualify through one command does not preclude direct contribution or indirect contribution through another qualifying downstream write.

We next determine which qualifying consumers ultimately contribute to verification. For this purpose, we construct a separate reachability graph GEG_{E}. It contains agent-command nodes and an endpoint representing EE, but excludes the verifier command itself. A qualifying consumption creates an edge from the earlier writer to the later writer, while write commands with directly contributing records are connected to EE. Matching non-file resource events provide the corresponding endpoint connections.

Let 𝒮E\mathcal{S}_{E} denote the set of write commands that have a directed path to EE in GEG_{E}. A written record (p,ℓ)(p,\ell) of command cc is therefore counted as an indirect contribution if at least one of its qualifying downstream consumers belongs to 𝒮E\mathcal{S}_{E}:

Ic={(p,ℓ)∈𝒲c:𝒰c​(p,ℓ)∩𝒮E≠∅},𝒲cE=Dc∪Ic.\displaystyle I_{c}=\{(p,\ell)\in\mathcal{W}_{c}:\mathcal{U}_{c}(p,\ell)\cap\mathcal{S}_{E}\neq\varnothing\},\qquad\mathcal{W}_{c}^{E}=D_{c}\cup I_{c}. (13)

Here, IcI_{c} contains the indirectly contributing records of cc, while 𝒲cE\mathcal{W}_{c}^{E} combines its direct and indirect contributions. Because this combination is a set union, a record that satisfies both conditions is counted only once.

Operationally, reverse traversal starts from writes connected to resources in EE and repeatedly follows qualifying input relations to earlier writers until no additional writers are found. The input reads of a write command are used only to trace contributions of earlier writes; the command itself remains scored by the write-credit rule.

Each tracked record contributes at most once to 𝒲cE\mathcal{W}_{c}^{E}, even if it has multiple qualifying consumers or satisfies both the direct and indirect conditions. An input record is attributed to its earlier writer, whereas a downstream output record belongs to the later writer, and each command is normalized by its own set 𝒲c\mathcal{W}_{c}. Qualifying records are not weighted by the contribution scores of downstream writers, and no distance decay is applied in the write-reachability calculation.

A.4 Complete Command Credit

For a write command with tracked file records, the contribution score is the fraction of its written records that contribute to EE. The denominator is the number of tracked records produced by that command, rather than the size of any file it reads or edits. When line-level ranges are unavailable, WHOLE_FILE=−1=-1 is treated as one tracked record and therefore remains in the file-based branch. The complete write credit is

q⁡(c)=Contrib⁡(c)={|𝒲cE|/|𝒲c|,|𝒲c|>0,1,|𝒲c|=0​and​c∈𝒮E,0,otherwise.\displaystyle q(c)=\operatorname{Contrib}(c)=\begin{cases}|\mathcal{W}_{c}^{E}|/|\mathcal{W}_{c}|,&|\mathcal{W}_{c}|>0,\\ 1,&|\mathcal{W}_{c}|=0\ \text{and}\ c\in\mathcal{S}_{E},\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (14)

The second branch applies to write commands with no tracked file record that nevertheless reach EE, such as commands represented only by port or process events. For such non-file resources, a match with a verifier-inspected resource gives credit one and no match gives zero. If a command already has a file-based contribution score, a matching non-file resource does not replace that score, preserving the graded file contribution for commands with mixed resource records.

For a read command rr, let 𝒟G​(r)\mathcal{D}_{G}(r) denote the set of agent write commands reachable from rr in GG, excluding the verifier. Let dG​(r,c)d_{G}(r,c) be the shortest directed path length from rr to a reachable write cc. Its raw credit is

q⁡(r)=∑c∈𝒟G​(r)βdG​(r,c)​Contrib⁡(c),β∈(0,1].\displaystyle q(r)=\sum\nolimits_{c\in\mathcal{D}_{G}(r)}\beta^{d_{G}(r,c)}\operatorname{Contrib}(c),\qquad\beta\in(0,1]. (15)

Each reachable write contributes at most one term, with the shortest path determining the decay when multiple paths connect rr to the same write. Contributions from distinct writes are summed, so read credit may exceed one. A read command with no path to any positive-credit write receives zero.

Both write and read credits are nonnegative scores that quantify recorded relevance to verification rather than trajectory success. They determine where the learning signal is assigned, while the signed group-relative advantage determines whether the corresponding sampled responses are reinforced or penalized. Thus, high credit identifies greater recorded relevance without implying that the associated content is correct.

A.5 Advantage Redistribution and Policy Objective

From command credits to step factors. Each traced command receives either write credit or read credit according to the rules above. Let 𝒞i,t\mathcal{C}_{i,t} contain all traced commands in step tt of trajectory τi\tau_{i}, and let 𝒮i={t:𝒞i,t≠∅}\mathcal{S}_{i}=\{t:\mathcal{C}_{i,t}\neq\varnothing\} denote the set of steps containing at least one traced command. We aggregate command credits within each step as

qi,t=∑c∈𝒞i,tq⁡(c),\displaystyle q_{i,t}=\sum\nolimits_{c\in\mathcal{C}_{i,t}}q(c), (16)

where q⁡(c)q(c) denotes the write or read credit assigned to command cc according to its command type. Credits from multiple commands in the same step are summed rather than averaged. The resulting step credits are compared only within the same trajectory.

For nonempty 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i}, define

mi=mins∈𝒮i⁡qi,s,Δi=∑s∈𝒮i(qi,s−mi).\displaystyle m_{i}=\min_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}q_{i,s},\qquad\Delta_{i}=\sum\nolimits_{s\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}(q_{i,s}-m_{i}). (17)

The step factors are then

fi,t={|𝒮i|​(qi,t−mi)/Δi,t∈𝒮i,Δi>10−9,1,otherwise.\displaystyle f_{i,t}=\begin{cases}|\mathcal{S}_{i}|(q_{i,t}-m_{i})/\Delta_{i},&t\in\mathcal{S}_{i},\ \Delta_{i}>10^{-9},\\ 1,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} (18)

Thus, when the compared step credits are nondegenerate, subtracting mim_{i} uses the lowest observed credit as the within-trajectory reference, while division by Δi/|𝒮i|\Delta_{i}/|\mathcal{S}_{i}| normalizes the mean factor over 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} to one. The minimum-credit steps therefore receive factor zero, even when their raw credits are positive.

Steps without traced commands retain an initial factor of one and are not included in the within-trajectory comparison. If 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} is empty, tracing yields no usable credit, or Δi≤10−9\Delta_{i}\leq 10^{-9}, all step factors are set to one and the baseline advantage assignment is retained. In particular, if no write command has positive contribution to EE, all write credits are zero and the propagated read credits are also zero, triggering the same fallback.

From step factors to final weights and advantages. Let Mi,j∈{0,1}M_{i,j}\in\{0,1\} indicate whether token position jj enters the policy loss. Policy-generated tokens have mask one, while environment observations have mask zero. The factor of step tt is assigned to the corresponding policy-generated token span. Positions outside the mapped spans retain an initial factor of one; if such positions enter the loss, they are included in the subsequent token-level normalization.

Because the policy loss averages over generated tokens, steps with longer responses contribute more loss terms. We therefore normalize the step factors by their token-weighted mean. When all included tokens are covered by mapped step spans, let Li,tL_{i,t} denote the number of loss-included tokens from step tt. For positive included length and normalization denominator,

Zi=∑t=1TiLi,t​fi,t∑t=1TiLi,t,wi,t=fi,tZi,A^i,tDep=wi,t​A^i.\displaystyle Z_{i}=\frac{\sum\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{i}}L_{i,t}f_{i,t}}{\sum\nolimits_{t=1}^{T_{i}}L_{i,t}},\qquad w_{i,t}=\frac{f_{i,t}}{Z_{i}},\qquad\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{Dep}}_{i,t}=w_{i,t}\widehat{A}_{i}. (19)

Here, fi,tf_{i,t} is the step factor before token-level normalization, wi,tw_{i,t} is the final weight, and A^i,tDep\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{Dep}}_{i,t} is the redistributed advantage for step tt. Every loss-included token in that step receives the same redistributed advantage. A step without traced commands has fi,t=1f_{i,t}=1 before token-level normalization and therefore receives final weight 1/Zi1/Z_{i}, which is not necessarily one.

In the implementation, ZiZ_{i} is computed directly over all policy-generated tokens included in the loss. Each token inherits the factor of its mapped interaction step; any included token without a valid step mapping retains the default factor of one. When every included token is mapped to a step, this token-level computation reduces exactly to the expression above.

What normalization preserves. For a nondegenerate step-level redistribution,

∑t∈𝒮ifi,t=|𝒮i|.\displaystyle\sum_{t\in\mathcal{S}_{i}}f_{i,t}=|\mathcal{S}_{i}|. (20)

Since steps outside 𝒮i\mathcal{S}_{i} retain factor one, the mean step factor over the trajectory is also one. After token-level normalization,

∑tLi,t​wi,t∑tLi,t=1,∑tLi,t​A^i,tDep∑tLi,t=A^i.\displaystyle\frac{\sum_{t}L_{i,t}w_{i,t}}{\sum_{t}L_{i,t}}=1,\qquad\frac{\sum_{t}L_{i,t}\widehat{A}^{\mathrm{Dep}}_{i,t}}{\sum_{t}L_{i,t}}=\widehat{A}_{i}. (21)

Thus, the step-level normalization preserves the mean step factor, while the token-level normalization preserves the token-weighted mean final weight. Consequently, the token-weighted mean redistributed advantage remains equal to the original group-relative advantage A^i\widehat{A}_{i}.

These identities apply to the advantage coefficients rather than to the resulting optimization dynamics. The policy gradient, its norm, and the clipped objective may still change because different tokens receive different coefficients. In particular, unequal response lengths can yield Zi≠1Z_{i}\neq 1 even when the unweighted mean step factor is one.

All valid weights are nonnegative and therefore preserve the sign of A^i\widehat{A}_{i}. If A^i=0\widehat{A}_{i}=0, all redistributed advantages remain zero. DepGPO therefore redistributes the learning signal supplied by the GRPO baseline without creating a nonzero signal when the original group-relative advantage is zero.

Policy objective. Index all policy-generated tokens included in a training minibatch by n=1,…,Nn=1,\ldots,N. Let yny_{n} denote token nn, hnh_{n} its original context, and ana_{n} the redistributed advantage of the interaction step containing that token. The corresponding probability ratio is

ρn​(θ)=πθ​(yn∣hn)πθold​(yn∣hn),\displaystyle\rho_{n}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}(y_{n}\mid h_{n})}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}(y_{n}\mid h_{n})}, (22)

where πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}} is the policy used to collect the trajectories. This indexing affects only the loss reduction; each token retains the context of its original trajectory.

Following the clipped surrogate update of the GRPO baseline, we define

ℓclip​(ρ,a)\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}(\rho,a) =min⁡{ρ​a,clip⁡(ρ,1−ϵlo,1+ϵhi)​a},\displaystyle=\min\!\left\{\rho a,\,\operatorname{clip}(\rho,1-\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}},1+\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}})a\right\},
ℓdc​(ρ,a)\displaystyle\ell_{\mathrm{dc}}(\rho,a) ={max⁡{ℓclip​(ρ,a),η​a},a<0,ℓclip​(ρ,a),a≥0,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\max\!\left\{\ell_{\mathrm{clip}}(\rho,a),\eta a\right\},&a<0,\\ \ell_{\mathrm{clip}}(\rho,a),&a\geq 0,\end{cases} (23)
ℒDep​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Dep}}(\theta) =−1N∑n=1Nℓdc(ρn(θ),an).\displaystyle=-\frac{1}{N}\sum\nolimits_{n=1}^{N}\ell_{\mathrm{dc}}(\rho_{n}(\theta),a_{n}). (24)

Here, ϵlo\epsilon_{\mathrm{lo}} and ϵhi\epsilon_{\mathrm{hi}} define the lower and upper clipping ranges, and η>1\eta>1 is the dual-clipping threshold for negative advantages. The dependency-derived factors and redistributed advantages are held fixed during each policy update. DepGPO changes only the advantages assigned to tokens, while retaining the clipping rule and token-mean reduction of the GRPO baseline.

Fallback and integration. Table 4 summarizes the conditions under which unit dependency factors are used. Step factors are derived from the rollout records, expanded to the corresponding token positions, and normalized using the policy-loss mask. The resulting weights are applied after the baseline group-relative advantages are computed and before the actor update. The current integration also applies the same weights to the returns tensor. Because the GRPO path used here is critic-free, this does not introduce a separate critic target; the returns tensor carries the same outcome-derived signal used by the policy update.

A.6 End-to-End Procedure

The following procedure summarizes the complete DepGPO training pipeline. Resource extraction and dependency-based credit assignment are computed from the recorded trajectories and are held fixed during the corresponding policy updates.

  1. 1.

    Sample KK trajectories for each task using πθold\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}, recording step-to-command mappings and policy-generated token spans.

  2. 2.

    Execute the task verifier for each trajectory to obtain the terminal reward RiR_{i} and the verifier resource-access records.

  3. 3.

    For each trajectory, extract the verifier endpoint set EE, construct the command dependency graph GG, and build the qualifying write-consumption relations that define GEG_{E}.

  4. 4.

    Traverse GEG_{E} backward from EE to identify directly and indirectly contributing write records, count each qualifying record once, and compute write credit.

  5. 5.

    For each read command, identify reachable write descendants in GG and sum their contribution scores with shortest-path decay to obtain read credit.

  6. 6.

    Aggregate command credits within each interaction step, compute the corresponding step factors, and apply the documented unit-factor fallbacks when necessary.

  7. 7.

    Expand the step factors to policy-generated tokens and normalize them over the policy-loss mask to obtain the final weights. After the baseline group-relative advantages are computed, apply these weights to obtain the redistributed per-step advantages.

  8. 8.

    Update the policy parameters θ\theta using Eq. 24, and then collect the next group of trajectories with the updated policy.

Appendix B Experimental Setup and Reproducibility

This appendix provides the complete experimental setup used to evaluate DepGPO and the baselines, with particular attention to training consistency, comparison fairness, and reproducibility. We first describe the common training pipeline and controlled settings shared across methods, followed by the training data, task selection and splits, model configurations, optimization hyperparameters, evaluation protocol, and implementation details.

All methods follow the same two-stage training procedure, consisting of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on terminal trajectories followed by reinforcement learning (RL) on selected training tasks. SETA (Shen et al., 2026) and TMAX (Ivison et al., 2026) are used separately with Qwen3.5-9B (Qwen Team, 2026a) and Qwen3.6-27B (Qwen Team, 2026b). Within each model and data setting, all methods share the same SFT checkpoint, selected task pool, training and validation split, and agent scaffold, ensuring matched starting policies and task distributions. For the direct comparison between GRPO and DepGPO, we additionally keep the policy objective and optimization settings unchanged, with DepGPO modifying only how the group-relative advantage is redistributed across interaction steps. Other baselines retain their respective method-specific algorithmic components while using the same shared experimental setting whenever applicable.

B.1 Supervised Fine-Tuning

We fine-tune each base model on SETA and TMAX separately, producing an SFT checkpoint for the corresponding RL setting. The SFT configuration uses AdamW with a learning rate of 10−510^{-5}, optimizer coefficients (0.9,0.95)(0.9,0.95), weight decay 0.010.01, and gradient clipping at 1.01.0. The learning rate increases during the first 3%3\% of training and remains constant afterward. Each run completes one epoch over its training corpus.

Training updates all model parameters in bfloat16 and uses Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP), gradient checkpointing, and sequence packing. Multi-turn conversations are tokenized with the preceding context retained, while the loss includes only assistant tokens. Conversations exceeding the sequence limit are truncated from the left. Table 5 summarizes the corpus sizes and sequence limits. SETA and TMAX use different sequence budgets, while the settings share the optimizer configuration above. The conversation counts refer to SFT examples and are distinct from the task counts used for RL.

B.2 Selecting Training Tasks

With binary outcome rewards, a sampled group containing only successes or only failures has zero centered group-relative advantages. Such groups therefore provide no outcome-based policy-gradient signal for GRPO or for DepGPO’s redistribution of those advantages. To increase the frequency of informative groups, we select tasks on which the corresponding SFT policy produces both successful and unsuccessful attempts.

For each candidate task xx, we sample four trajectories with the SFT checkpoint of that model and data setting. Let zx,k∈{0,1}z_{x,k}\in\{0,1\} be the verifier outcome of attempt kk. We compute

p^SFT​(x)=14​∑k=14zx,k,𝒫={x:0<p^SFT​(x)<1},\displaystyle\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(x)=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{k=1}^{4}z_{x,k},\qquad\mathcal{P}=\{x:0<\widehat{p}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(x)<1\}, (25)

where 𝒫\mathcal{P} denotes the retained task pool. With four attempts, this rule retains success rates of 0.250.25, 0.500.50, and 0.750.75. Tasks with zero or four successful attempts are excluded. The retained pool is then fixed across all RL methods in that setting. This selection increases the availability of mixed-outcome tasks under the initial policy, although later training groups can still contain identical rewards.

For SETA/9B, the excluded groups contain 639+200=839639+200=839 tasks, accounting for approximately 61%61\% of the 1,3761{,}376 candidates. This is the proportion reported in the pilot analysis. On the same candidate collection, the 27B checkpoint produces fewer zero-success groups and more four-success groups, leaving 596596 tasks for RL. Because selection depends on the initial policy, task pools are constructed separately for each model and data setting. Fairness across methods is maintained by reusing the same pool within a setting.

In the TMAX completion, the 9B counts retain 540 of 2,998 tasks (18.01%), while the 27B counts retain 648 tasks (21.61%). The 27B pool contains 583 training tasks and 65 validation tasks after the same deterministic split.

We split each retained pool by sorting task identifiers and assigning the first ⌊0.9​|𝒫|⌋\lfloor 0.9|\mathcal{P}|\rfloor tasks to RL training and the remainder to RL validation. This deterministic rule gives the counts in Table 6. The RL validation tasks are held out from policy updates and are used for checkpoint selection. They are separate from the conversation-level validation splits listed for SFT.

B.3 Reinforcement Learning

RL starts from the SFT checkpoint corresponding to the model and training source. Each update samples four training tasks and eight trajectories per task, giving 32 trajectories. The training budget is 150 policy updates. Table 7 gives the common settings for the controlled GRPO and DepGPO comparison, including the settings that differ across model sizes or training sources.

Across all settings, each update samples four tasks with K=8K=8 trajectories per task, yielding 32 trajectories, and training runs for 150 policy updates. We use AdamW with a learning rate of 10−610^{-6}, a constant schedule, clipping range (0.2,0.28)(0.2,0.28), dual-clip threshold η=3.0\eta=3.0, no KL penalty or entropy bonus, group-SD normalization, a response-token budget of 24,576, and β=0.5\beta=0.5 for DepGPO. The SETA settings allow up to 10 interaction steps per trajectory, while TMAX uses 56, with sampling temperatures of 1.01.0 and 0.70.7, respectively. For Qwen3.5-9B, we use a 120-second command timeout and sequence-parallel degree one; Qwen3.6-27B uses a 400-second timeout and sequence-parallel degree four. All settings use four NVIDIA H200 GPUs.

A trajectory ends when the agent declares completion or reaches its interaction or token limit. The task verifier then returns a binary outcome, with no intermediate environment reward. DepGPO uses the command and verifier records to compute write and read credit, aggregates command credits into step factors, and normalizes those factors into final weights. The weights multiply the group-relative advantages before the policy update, following Appendix A.5. The outcome reward and the underlying policy objective remain unchanged in the GRPO comparison.

B.4 Checkpoint Selection

We periodically evaluate checkpoints on the RL validation tasks from the corresponding retained pool. For each method, we select the checkpoint with the highest validation success rate and use that checkpoint for the final benchmark evaluation. The same selection criterion applies to DepGPO and all baselines. Consequently, a baseline that deteriorates later in training can still be evaluated at an earlier checkpoint when that checkpoint has the highest validation score. The complete training curves are analyzed separately to assess training stability.

Checkpoint selection uses RL validation performance. Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1 scores are reserved for reporting the selected policies, with the data-separation protocol described in Appendix B.6.

B.5 Benchmark Evaluation and Score Aggregation

We evaluate the selected checkpoints separately on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1. Each attempt begins from the task’s initial environment and allows at most 56 interaction steps. We conduct five independent attempts per task and repeat the complete evaluation three times. Within each round, pass@1 is estimated by averaging the five binary outcomes for each task and then averaging across tasks.

For benchmark version vv, let JvJ_{v} be the number of tasks and let zj,h,a(v,m)∈{0,1}z_{j,h,a}^{(v,m)}\in\{0,1\} denote the outcome for method mm on task jj, evaluation round hh, and attempt aa. The task and benchmark scores for each round are

p^j,h(v,m)=15​∑a=15zj,h,a(v,m),sh(v,m)=100Jv​∑j=1Jvp^j,h(v,m).\displaystyle\widehat{p}_{j,h}^{(v,m)}=\frac{1}{5}\sum_{a=1}^{5}z_{j,h,a}^{(v,m)},\qquad s_{h}^{(v,m)}=\frac{100}{J_{v}}\sum_{j=1}^{J_{v}}\widehat{p}_{j,h}^{(v,m)}. (26)

With H=3H=3 evaluation rounds, we report

s¯(v,m)=1H​∑h=1Hsh(v,m),SD(v,m)=1H−1​∑h=1H(sh(v,m)−s¯(v,m))2.\displaystyle\overline{s}^{(v,m)}=\frac{1}{H}\sum_{h=1}^{H}s_{h}^{(v,m)},\qquad\operatorname{SD}^{(v,m)}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{H-1}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\left(s_{h}^{(v,m)}-\overline{s}^{(v,m)}\right)^{2}}. (27)

The table 1 show s¯±SD\overline{s}\pm\operatorname{SD} in percentage points. This SD measures evaluation variability for a fixed trained checkpoint. Variability across independently trained policies requires separate training runs. In addition, averaging individual attempts estimates pass@1; treating a task as solved whenever any of its five attempts succeeds would instead estimate pass@5.

B.6 Data Separation and Verifier Information

Task selection uses the training-source collections, and RL validation tasks are excluded from policy updates. Terminal-Bench evaluation tasks are kept separate from the training and validation task pools and are not used to choose checkpoints. Conversation-level SFT splits and task-level RL splits serve different purposes, so their separation is assessed at the appropriate unit.

After a training trajectory is completed, the task verifier returns the terminal outcome and records which resources it inspects. DepGPO uses these access records to construct EE and then computes the dependency-based weights for the finished trajectory. These weights are applied only after the trajectory has been generated; the policy does not receive EE or the verifier access records as additional input during action generation. Thus, DepGPO still learns from a terminal reward, while execution dependencies are used only to determine how that reward-derived advantage is distributed across steps. Whether the agent can directly access verifier scripts through the terminal is determined by the agent scaffold and is independent of this weighting procedure.

Appendix C Task-Level Paired Comparison

This appendix examines how the aggregate performance gains of DepGPO are distributed across individual tasks. We compare DepGPO and GRPO using Qwen3.5-9B trained on SETA, with evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 2.1. The analysis examines the frequency and magnitude of improvements, ties, and regressions.

Comparison protocol. For each benchmark version vv, we compare the two methods on the same 89 tasks. Let p¯j(v,m)\bar{p}_{j}^{(v,m)} denote the observed success rate of method mm on task jj, expressed as a proportion. The task-level difference and its benchmark average are

Δj(v)\displaystyle\Delta_{j}^{(v)} =100​(p¯j(v,DepGPO)−p¯j(v,GRPO)),\displaystyle=100\left(\bar{p}_{j}^{(v,\mathrm{DepGPO})}-\bar{p}_{j}^{(v,\mathrm{GRPO})}\right),
Δ¯(v)\displaystyle\overline{\Delta}^{(v)} =189​∑j=189Δj(v).\displaystyle=\frac{1}{89}\sum_{j=1}^{89}\Delta_{j}^{(v)}. (28)

Positive, zero, and negative differences indicate improvements, ties, and regressions, respectively. Figure 6 sorts tasks independently within each benchmark by descending Δj(v)\Delta_{j}^{(v)}. The horizontal axis therefore represents the rank of the observed difference, not task difficulty or a shared task ordering across benchmark versions.

Coverage of improvements. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, DepGPO improves on 31 tasks, ties on 53, and performs worse on 5, with a mean improvement of 14.2 percentage points (pp). On Terminal-Bench 2.1, the corresponding counts are 33, 54, and 2, with a mean improvement of 13.6 pp. Among tasks with nonzero differences, improvements account for 31 of 36 tasks (86.1%) on Terminal-Bench 2.0 and 33 of 35 tasks (94.3%) on Terminal-Bench 2.1. Thus, when the observed success rates differ, the difference predominantly favors DepGPO. These counts describe tasks with higher success rates, not necessarily tasks newly solved by DepGPO.

Magnitude of improvements and regressions. The positive differences vary substantially across tasks, with several large improvements alongside smaller gains. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, the highlighted examples include approximately 80 pp on extract-moves-from-video and 67 pp each on git-leak-recovery and pypi-server. On Terminal-Bench 2.1, git-leak-recovery improves by approximately 87 pp, while nginx-request-logging, openssl-selfsigned-cert, and sqlite-with-gcov each improve by approximately 73 pp. These examples show that substantial improvements occur on multiple tasks.

Regressions remain present and should be considered alongside these gains. On Terminal-Bench 2.0, the highlighted decreases are approximately 27 pp on vulnerable-secret and 13 pp on gpt2-codegolf. The latter also decreases by approximately 13 pp on Terminal-Bench 2.1. The positive benchmark averages therefore reflect improvements that outweigh the observed regressions, not uniform gains on every task.

Ties and differences between benchmark versions. Ties constitute the majority of tasks in both panels, giving a median task-level difference of zero despite the positive mean differences. The average improvement consequently summarizes gains on a subset of tasks, while many tasks retain the same observed success rate. A zero difference alone does not establish that a task is solved reliably: equal success rates can also reflect shared failures. Moreover, equal task-level success rates do not imply identical command sequences or execution dependencies.

Terminal-Bench 2.1 has two more improved tasks and three fewer regressed tasks than Terminal-Bench 2.0, yet its mean improvement is slightly smaller. This illustrates that the number of improved tasks and the magnitude of their improvements capture different aspects of performance. The two benchmarks show a similar overall pattern, but the independently sorted panels do not establish that the same tasks improve in both versions.

Relation to dependency-aware credit assignment. These task-level results are consistent with the motivation of DepGPO. Its credit rules distinguish writes connected to verifier-inspected resources and assign credit to the reads and earlier writes that support them. This redistribution may help on tasks where useful information and intermediate outputs pass through several commands, because those dependencies provide a basis for assigning the group-relative learning signal. However, the outcome differences alone do not identify which dependency paths explain an individual task’s improvement or regression; that attribution requires inspecting its execution traces.

Overall, the paired comparison complements aggregate pass@1 by showing that DepGPO improves substantially more tasks than it degrades, with several large gains and many unchanged outcomes. These results support task-dependent benefits for Qwen3.5-9B trained on SETA, without implying universal improvement or statistical significance for every individual task.

Appendix D Additional Training Stability Analysis

This appendix provides additional analysis of the training behavior shown in Figure 5. We clarify the diagnostic signals used in the figure and examine how training reward, policy entropy, gradient norm, and dependency-based credit redistribution evolve during optimization. Panels (a)–(c) compare DepGPO, GRPO, and GiGPO using Qwen3.5-9B trained on SETA. Panel (d) compares the evolution of DepGPO’s step-factor dispersion for Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B, both trained on SETA. For visualization, all training curves are smoothed using a centered moving average over up to 11 adjacent training steps, with truncated windows at the boundaries. Policy entropy is smoothed in log10\log_{10} space and then transformed back to its original scale, while all other metrics are smoothed on their original scales. Checkpoint selection is conducted independently using the RL validation protocol described in Appendix B.4.

D.1 Diagnostics and Plotting Protocol

The four diagnostics in Figure 5 capture complementary aspects of training. Training reward reflects the terminal verifier outcomes obtained by the sampled trajectories at each policy update. Policy entropy characterizes the concentration of the policy distribution over generated tokens, while gradient norm measures the magnitude of the actor update. For DepGPO, we additionally report the standard deviation of the step factors, which measures how differently the group-relative advantage is allocated across interaction steps.

For visualization, all training curves are smoothed using a centered moving average over up to 11 adjacent training steps, with truncated windows at the boundaries. Policy entropy is smoothed in log10\log_{10} space and then transformed back to its original scale, while all other metrics are smoothed on their original scales. The shaded late-training region highlights the stage in which the methods exhibit clearly different optimization behavior; it does not affect training or checkpoint selection. Policy entropy is shown on a logarithmic scale to make variation in low-entropy regimes more visible.

D.2 Training Reward Dynamics

Figure 5(a) shows distinct late-training behavior across the three methods. GRPO improves during the earlier stage but subsequently loses much of this gain, while GiGPO deteriorates earlier and remains at a comparatively low reward level. DepGPO instead fluctuates while maintaining an overall higher reward during the late stage.

These differences are consistent with the credit-assignment mechanisms of the three methods. GRPO assigns the same group-relative advantage to all generated steps in a trajectory. Consequently, commands with weak or no recorded connection to the verified outcome can receive the same signed learning signal as commands that directly support task completion.

GiGPO introduces step-level credit through comparisons among actions associated with matching environment states. However, as shown by the pilot analysis in Figure 1, repeated states are sparse in the terminal setting considered here, limiting the number of additional step groups that can be formed. DepGPO does not require such state recurrence. Instead, it uses observed read–write dependencies within each trajectory to determine where the available group-relative advantage is applied.

The reward curves therefore provide evidence that DepGPO maintains stronger late-stage training performance in the runs shown. They do not by themselves establish that credit assignment is the only cause of the observed degradation of the baselines.

D.3 Policy Entropy and Gradient Norm

The entropy curves provide a complementary view of how the policies evolve. As shown in Figure 5(b), GiGPO exhibits an early increase followed by a sharp decline in policy entropy. GRPO follows a different pattern, with entropy increasing substantially later in training. DepGPO remains comparatively stable over the same training horizon.

The gradient statistics show a corresponding difference in optimization behavior. In Figure 5(c), both baselines exhibit very small gradients during the later stage, whereas DepGPO continues to receive nonzero updates. In the unsmoothed logs, the GRPO gradient norm is exactly zero on 43 of the final 45 updates. Together with the reward curves, this indicates that the baseline runs enter late-training regimes in which further policy updates provide limited effective learning, while DepGPO continues to update.

Entropy and gradient norm should not be interpreted as performance metrics in isolation. A particular entropy value is not inherently preferable, and a larger gradient norm does not necessarily imply a better policy. Their relevance here lies in their temporal relationship with the reward curves: the baseline reward degradation coincides with substantial changes in policy entropy and diminishing gradients, whereas DepGPO exhibits less pronounced degeneration across these diagnostics.

D.4 Evolution of Credit Redistribution

Figure 5(d) examines DepGPO’s redistribution mechanism directly. For each trajectory, command-level credit is aggregated into step factors fi,tf_{i,t}. As defined in Appendix A.5, these factors are normalized so that their mean across interaction steps is one. The mean therefore does not indicate how unevenly the learning signal is distributed, motivating the use of the step-factor standard deviation.

A small standard deviation indicates relatively similar weights across interaction steps, whereas a larger value indicates a more differentiated allocation. For both Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.6-27B trained on SETA, the step-factor standard deviation generally becomes larger later in training, although the trajectories fluctuate across updates. This pattern indicates that DepGPO increasingly differentiates among interaction steps as optimization proceeds.

The increasing dispersion should not be interpreted as an increase in the overall magnitude of the learning signal. The step-level normalization fixes the mean factor at one, while the subsequent token-level normalization preserves the token-weighted mean redistributed advantage. Thus, the change in standard deviation reflects a change in where the group-relative learning signal is allocated rather than a uniform amplification of that signal.

The 9B and 27B curves also show that differentiated credit allocation is observed at both model scales. Their exact trajectories need not match: model capacity, sampled trajectories, and the dependency structures observed during training can all affect the distribution of step credit. Accordingly, Figure 5(d) is used as a descriptive comparison rather than evidence that model size alone causes the difference between the two curves.

D.5 Relationship Between Credit Redistribution and Stability

Taken together, the diagnostics show a consistent pattern in the analyzed runs. DepGPO maintains higher late-stage training reward and nonzero policy updates while its step-level allocation becomes increasingly differentiated. This behavior is consistent with the intended role of dependency-aware credit assignment: the group-relative advantage determines whether a trajectory is reinforced or penalized, while execution dependencies determine how strongly that signal is assigned to different interaction steps.

The normalization procedure is important for this interpretation. Because the mean step factor is fixed and token-level normalization preserves the average advantage scale, the observed stability cannot be explained simply by a uniform increase in the original GRPO learning signal. DepGPO instead changes the relative contribution of tokens from different interaction steps while preserving the sign and overall scale of the trajectory-level advantage.

These observations establish an association between dependency-aware redistribution and more stable late-stage optimization in the runs examined here. They do not establish that any individual dependency edge, command credit, or step factor causally determines a particular change in reward, entropy, or gradient norm. Such causal attribution would require interventions on individual trajectories or dependency paths. The purpose of this analysis is therefore to characterize the optimization behavior accompanying DepGPO and to complement the final benchmark results in Table 1.

Appendix E Sensitivity and Computational Cost

This appendix examines the sensitivity of DepGPO to the dependency-decay coefficient β\beta and characterizes the additional computation introduced by dependency tracing and credit assignment. Unless otherwise specified, we use Qwen3.5-9B trained on SETA, matching the controlled setting used for the main ablation and stability analyses.

E.1 Sensitivity to Dependency Decay

The coefficient β\beta controls how quickly read credit decays with dependency distance. Smaller values emphasize reads that are close to relevant writes, whereas larger values retain more credit along longer dependency paths. We vary β\beta while keeping the remaining training configuration unchanged.

Performance remains relatively stable across a broad range of decay strengths. Moderate decay performs best in this setting, with β=0.5\beta=0.5 reaching 25.24/24.64 on Terminal-Bench 2.0/2.1. Reducing the coefficient to β=0.25\beta=0.25 yields 24.27/23.75, suggesting that overly rapid decay can suppress useful information propagated through multi-command dependency paths. Increasing the coefficient to β=0.75\beta=0.75 produces 24.87/24.12, remaining close to the default setting, whereas removing distance attenuation with β=1.0\beta=1.0 decreases performance to 23.97/23.45.

These results suggest that the benefit of DepGPO does not depend on a narrowly tuned decay value. At the same time, some attenuation is useful: assigning nearly equal importance to both short and long dependency paths can increase the influence of more distant supporting reads, while overly aggressive decay can remove informative longer-range dependencies. We therefore use β=0.5\beta=0.5 as a balanced default throughout the main experiments.

E.2 Computational Overhead

DepGPO introduces additional computation after trajectory execution. For each completed trajectory, the implementation parses the recorded resource accesses, constructs the command dependency graph, traces verifier-relevant writes, propagates credit to supporting reads, and maps the resulting step factors back to policy-generated tokens. These operations use the recorded execution trace and require no additional language-model forward or backward passes.

Table 10 compares the resulting cost with GRPO under the same Qwen3.5-9B and SETA training configuration. Wall-clock measurements include rollout collection, dependency processing, and the policy update.

The additional wall-clock cost is modest relative to the complete terminal-agent training loop. DepGPO increases the average update time by approximately 7.0%, while peak GPU memory changes by only 1.0%. This difference reflects the fact that dependency construction and credit computation operate primarily on execution records rather than model activations. The additional processing takes approximately 3.8 seconds per trajectory in this setting and does not introduce extra language-model inference.

The overhead is therefore concentrated in trace processing rather than neural network computation. This distinction is particularly relevant for terminal tasks, where rollout execution itself includes repeated environment interactions and command execution. As a result, dependency analysis contributes only a limited fraction of the overall training time.

E.3 Dependency-Trace Statistics

We further examine how frequently the dependency mechanism is active during training. Table 11 summarizes execution-trace statistics collected from the Qwen3.5-9B SETA run. These statistics describe the traces used for credit assignment before token-level normalization.

Usable dependency credit is available for 82.4% of trajectories, indicating that the redistribution mechanism is active for most sampled interactions rather than being dominated by fallback cases. Only 17.6% of trajectories revert to unit factors because no usable relative credit can be constructed.

Both components of the credit mechanism are exercised frequently. Approximately 38.7% of traced write commands receive positive credit, while 27.9% of read commands receive positive supporting-read credit. This indicates that the resulting signal is not restricted to direct environment-modifying operations: a substantial fraction of information-gathering commands can be connected to later verifier-relevant writes.

Indirect contribution is also non-negligible. Among positive-credit writes, 18.6% receive at least part of their credit through downstream write dependencies. This supports the distinction between direct persistence in verifier-inspected resources and earlier writes whose information is consumed by later relevant commands. The mean shortest distance from a credited read to its reachable writes is 1.74 dependency edges, showing that supporting information commonly extends beyond an immediately adjacent command.

E.4 Summary

Overall, the sensitivity analysis indicates that DepGPO remains effective across a range of dependency-decay coefficients, with moderate decay providing the strongest performance in the examined setting. The trace statistics further show that dependency-based redistribution is applicable to most training trajectories and frequently assigns credit to both relevant writes and supporting reads. At the same time, the additional computation remains small relative to the full terminal-agent training loop because the method operates on recorded execution traces and requires no additional model evaluations. Together, these results suggest that the dependency mechanism provides fine-grained credit assignment without introducing a large computational burden.

Appendix F Qualitative Credit-Assignment Examples

This appendix illustrates how DepGPO assigns credit in individual terminal trajectories. We present three representative cases covering supporting reads, indirect write contributions, and commands that receive no credit because they do not contribute to verifier-inspected resources. The first and third examples are rollouts of the Qwen3.5-9B agent used in our pilot study, while the second is a reference solution executed under the same tracer. All command credits are computed using the same implementation and β=0.5\beta=0.5 as in training.

The tables show selected commands rather than complete trajectories. Raw command credit q⁡(c)q(c) is computed from the complete recorded trace. During training, these credits are subsequently aggregated into step factors and token-normalized weights as described in Appendix A.

F.1 Supporting Reads

The first example shows why a command can receive credit even when it does not modify the environment. In count-dataset-tokens, the agent must compute the number of tokens in a specified subset of a dataset and write the result to /app/answer.txt. In the trajectory shown below, a Python command computes and prints 63841, after which the next command writes that value to the answer file. The verifier expects a different total, so the trajectory fails. One of the four trajectories in its rollout group succeeds, giving this trajectory a negative group-relative advantage of A^=−0.58\hat{A}=-0.58.

Although t17t_{17} records no file write, its standard output is used directly by the following write:

t17→stdout: 63841t18⟶E.t_{17}\xrightarrow{\ \text{stdout: }\texttt{63841}\ }t_{18}\longrightarrow E.

Because t18t_{18} receives full write credit, t17t_{17} receives supporting-read credit

q⁡(t17)=β​q​(t18)=0.5.q(t_{17})=\beta\,q(t_{18})=0.5.

By contrast, t19t_{19} reads the answer only after it has been written. No later positive-credit write depends on this read, so it receives zero credit. The example therefore distinguishes a read that helps produce a relevant write from a read that merely inspects the resulting state.

Because the trajectory has a negative group-relative advantage, the dependency-derived factors do not turn these credits into rewards. Instead, they determine where the negative learning signal is concentrated. The direction of the update still comes from the trajectory outcome.

F.2 Indirect Write Contribution

The second example shows why a write can matter even when the file it creates is never inspected by the verifier. In bn-fit-modify, the task requires learning and modifying a Bayesian network and producing three CSV files checked by the verifier. The reference solution first writes an R script, modify_bn.R, and then executes that script to produce the required outputs.

The script written by t3t_{3} is not itself in EE. However, all 102 tracked lines are still available when t4t_{4} reads the script, and t4t_{4} writes different files that reach EE. The resulting dependency is

t3→file: modify_bn.Rt4⟶E.t_{3}\xrightarrow{\ \text{file: }\texttt{modify\_bn.R}\ }t_{4}\longrightarrow E.

All tracked lines written by t3t_{3} therefore qualify as indirect contributions:

Contrib⁡(t3)=102102=1.\mathrm{Contrib}(t_{3})=\frac{102}{102}=1.

The execution step t4t_{4} receives direct write credit because its outputs are among the resources inspected by the verifier.

The package-installation command in t2t_{2} modifies only system-library locations outside the traced task resources and has no recorded dependency to EE, so it receives zero credit.

This case captures an important pattern in terminal workflows. Scripts, temporary files, and intermediate configurations may disappear before verification while still determining the contents of the final outputs. Restricting credit to writes that persist directly in EE would miss such intermediate contributions.

F.3 Overwritten and Irrelevant Commands

The final example illustrates how a successful trajectory can contain both useful and unnecessary operations. In constraints-scheduling, the agent must read three calendars and write a meeting satisfying the required constraints to /app/meeting_scheduled.ics. Two of the four trajectories in the rollout group succeed, giving the trajectory shown here a positive group-relative advantage of A^=+1.00\hat{A}=+1.00.

During the trajectory, the agent writes an initial version of the output, reads it back, deletes it, writes another version, reads that version, and later writes the final output.

The first version written in t4t_{4} is removed before it contributes to a qualifying downstream write or remains in the final inspected state. It therefore receives zero credit. Similarly, the read-backs in t5t_{5} and t8t_{8} inspect the agent’s own output but do not support a later positive-credit write.

In contrast, the relevant records produced by t7t_{7} and t10t_{10} reach the final verifier-inspected file and receive full write credit. Thus, even within a successful trajectory, DepGPO does not automatically treat every action as equally responsible for the outcome.

This distinction is particularly important for long terminal trajectories, which often contain exploration, discarded edits, repeated inspections, and failed intermediate attempts. Uniform trajectory-level credit assigns the same positive signal to all of these operations, whereas dependency-aware credit separates commands connected to the verified state from those without such recorded connections.

F.4 From Command Credit to the Training Signal

The three examples illustrate complementary parts of the credit-assignment mechanism. Direct write credit identifies modifications that reach verifier-inspected resources. Indirect write credit recovers earlier modifications whose information is consumed by later relevant writes. Supporting-read credit extends attribution to information-gathering commands that enable those writes.

Raw command credits are first aggregated within each interaction step. DepGPO then normalizes the resulting step credits into nonnegative step factors and performs the token-level normalization described in Appendix A. If wi,tw_{i,t} is the resulting final weight, the advantage assigned to tokens in step tt is

A^i,tDep=wi,t​A^i.\hat{A}^{\mathrm{Dep}}_{i,t}=w_{i,t}\hat{A}_{i}.

The dependency-derived weights are nonnegative, so they change the magnitude but not the sign of the original group-relative advantage. When A^i>0\hat{A}_{i}>0, larger dependency weights strengthen reinforcement on the corresponding steps; when A^i<0\hat{A}_{i}<0, they strengthen the penalty. If A^i=0\hat{A}_{i}=0, all redistributed advantages remain zero. Among traced steps, lower dependency credit leads to smaller relative factors, while steps without traced operations retain the documented default factor.

Taken together, these examples show that DepGPO does not introduce a separate notion of task correctness at the command level. The terminal outcome still determines whether the trajectory is reinforced or penalized. Execution dependencies instead determine how that outcome-derived signal is distributed across the commands that produced the final state.
